body:
Several pressures shaping real estate fundraising are becoming more pronounced in 2026. Closed-end funds raised $81.7bn in H1, the third-lowest half-year total in more than a decade, while just 95 vehicles reached final close.

Launch activity reflects the same caution. Although 276 funds came to market, their combined $74.3bn target was the lowest since 2017, and capital continued to concentrate around the largest and most established managers.

Allocator interest remains more resilient and decisively tilted towards non-core strategies, which represented 70% of H1 intentions. Activity peaked in Q1 before slowing in Q2, while US public pensions dominated the ranking of the most active mandate issuers.

Pressure remains visible across open-end core funds and European real estate debt. Redemption queues have eased at several core vehicles but remain elevated at some funds. In European debt, large managers command most targeted capital, while smaller and emerging firms are increasingly turning to advisory work and institutional mandates.

Private wealth is becoming an increasingly important source of capital. BREIT still accounts for 60% of NAV across the 10 largest private REITs, although Blue Owl has overtaken Starwood to become the second-largest vehicle.

Fundraising sinks towards decade low

Geopolitical volatility and macroeconomic uncertainty led to the third lowest fundraising total in 10 years for a six-month period, with 95 closed-end real estate funds raising $81.7 billion. Only H1 and H2 2024 saw a more negative fundraising environment. This marks a reversal in industry sentiment compared to just six months ago before the US and Israeli attacks on Iran in February started another inflationary cycle that made investors review interest rate expectations and portfolio allocations accordingly.

Capital concentration remained a defining feature of real estate fundraising in H1 2026. The 10 largest funds accounted for 49% of total capital raised, while the top 20 funds accounted for 69% of total capital raised in the first six months of the year.

The importance of track record stands out even more in fundraising by series. Among the top 20 largest funds closed in H1 2026, only two – Digital Realty US Hyperscale Data Center Fund and Core Spaces Student Housing Fund – are first-time funds, signaling a strong investor appetite for these sectors. Across all funds closed in H1 2026, first-time vehicles accounted for only 17% of total capital raised over this period.

Fund launch targets fall to lowest since 2017

We tracked the lowest targeted amount of capital by real estate fund launches in a six-month period since 2017, with $74.3 billion of capital commitments targeted by 276 funds. 78% of targeted capital is directed towards value-add and opportunistic strategies.

Capital concentration is also reflected in the launch environment as 40% of targeted capital comes from the top 10 funds that have started raising money in the first six months of the year. 48% of targeted capital by real estate closed-end funds is directed towards diversified strategies. The largest launches in H1 include EQT Exeter’s latest industrial fund, Aermont’s latest flagship fund, and Ares Management’s new real estate secondaries fund.

Non-core strategies drive allocator activity

Real estate intentions spiked in the first quarter of 2026, amid allocator agreement that the recent market downturn had more or less bottomed out. Despite overtures about “green shoots” for core property in investor meetings, however, appetite remains decidedly with non-core, where alternative property types are more prevalent.

Recent moves by giants like CalPERS suggest non-core’s popularity will persist. In June, America’s largest public pension revealed plans to double the proportion of non-core strategies in its real estate portfolio by 2030. The announcement came after a decade of near abstention from non-core real estate by the $636 billion system.

While data centers remain popular among AI-conscious allocators, there is some trepidation about over-committing to such assets. In May, New Jersey Division of Investment CIO Shoaib Khan told us that manager expertise was crucial, given the sector’s rapidly evolving risks and massive demand for power. “We’re not gung-ho and saying ‘look, we need to pound the table on this’ because we do recognize the risk,” he said.

Aside from the AI boom, allocators continue to focus on demographic-driven strategies, particularly in residential property. Investors are increasingly bullish on senior housing strategies run by sector specialists that can source the right properties and operators.

Core funds work through redemption queues

Open-end core funds are still navigating choppy waters. Several funds were hit by underperformance, asset write-downs, liquidity issues and headwinds in the office and residential sectors, yet investors are showing signs of resilience in their allocation for core funds.

While some firms restructured their fund’s personnel team, others have implemented incentives to keep investors in the fund. Most of them, however, had to deal with significant portfolio alterations, with mixed results. Portfolio alternations focused primarily on rotating out of traditional core sectors like office, while increasing their exposure to alternative sectors such as healthcare real estate, student housing and some segments of the retail sector on top of the ever-increasing allocation to data centers.

Trumbull Property Fund’s redemption queue stood at 37% of NAV in Q1 2026—more than twice the 18% recorded by Invesco Core Real Estate, the next-highest fund.

Large managers dominate European debt pipeline

European real estate debt fundraising is substantial but heavily concentrated. We tracked 46 funds launched between 2022 and H1 2026, targeting €57 billion in aggregate. The 12 vehicles targeting at least €1 billion account for €41.8 billion, or 73% of the total. Brookfield’s €18 billion BSREP V and Blackstone’s €8 billion BREDS V together represent 46%.

This pipeline comes against AEW’s forecast €74 billion commercial real estate debt funding gap between 2026 and 2028. While the periods are not directly comparable, the estimate illustrates the opportunity that encouraged managers to establish or expand lending strategies.

However, several new and emerging participants have struggled. Chenavari launched a €500 million fund but later sold its interest to Atland subsidiary Aedgis. Schroders Capital targeted €1 billion before disbanding its European debt team after raising £100 million. Velo Capital launched two €500 million funds but closed only one, at €132 million, while Prime Capital raised €50 million against a €500 million target.

The result is an increasingly two-tier market. Established managers are securing the largest institutional commitments, while smaller firms are shifting towards advisory work and lending mandates. Former Prime Capital executive Guido Gerstner established MainCap to pursue international mandates, while Havenstone Capital moved away from its targeted €500m fund in favor of advisory opportunities.

German investor retreat hits European fundraising

European real estate fundraising has somewhat recovered from the lulls of 2023 and 2024, with $14.8 billion being raised in H1 2026. However, Scandinavian giants have still found the path to equity difficult.

Catella froze fundraising for two funds within the period, its targeted €500 million Catella European Affordable Housing Fund and its maiden €500 million Catella European Logistics Fund, citing lack of institutional investor appetite.

Niam has turned away from raising its first pan-Nordic debt fund, the targeted €500 million Niam Capital Solutions Fund I, also highlighting the lack of investor appetite.

Meanwhile, Urban Partners has only raised €132 million across its real estate debt suite, the targeted €500 million Velo Capital European Real Estate Debt Fund I and its €600 million Velo Mezzanine Credit Fund I.

Industry observers seem to agree that the common denominator are German institutional investors, with the Scandinavian real estate market being heavily reliant on capital from German investors whose lack of appetite has led to some of the largest Nordic managers scampering for equity.

BREIT dominates as Blue Owl moves into second

REITs showed signs of recovery in H1 2026, outpacing closed-end funds and posting some of the strongest returns in years driven by healthier valuations in real estate. Capital commitments coming from the private wealth channel keep contributing to the sector, with both non-traded NAV REITs and private placements attracting the lion’s share of fundraising.

The top 10 REITs grew to $95.6 billion total NAV in the first six months of the year. Most notably, Blue Owl Real Estate Net Lease Trust has surpassed Starwood Real Estate Income Trust as the second largest private REIT in the market behind Blackstone’s BREIT, which still represents 60% of the largest vehicles’ total NAV.

Redemption requests in BREIT keep declining, while Blue Owl’s REIT has been driving the majority of the firm’s fundraising following liquidity woes with its BDCs as accredited investors are attracted by the higher dividend yields and lower compliance costs found in a private placement structure despite its illiquidity.

On the other hand, Starwood had to suspend redemptions from SREIT to preserve liquidity. With 71% of its portfolio’s value being allocated to multi-family housing, specifically in the Sunbelt markets where rents have been relatively stagnant, the current environment demonstrates that allocators are prioritizing REITs that have quickly rotated their portfolios outside of traditional sectors.

Real estate fund managers are still tapping into the private wealth channel through interval funds, DSTs, OZ funds and, to a lesser extent, tender offer funds although none of these structures seem to attract the same level of interest from investors as REITs.

This report draws on proprietary With Intelligence by S&P Global data covering real estate fundraising, fund launches, investor intentions, institutional mandates, open-end core fund redemption queues, European real estate debt and non-traded REITs. Figures are based on data available through H1 or Q2 2026, with trends assessed against comparable historical periods where available.

With Intelligence is part of S&P Global, delivering end-to-end coverage across the alternatives marketplace. With Intelligence’s proprietary data spans a uniquely comprehensive view of private market activity and relationships, including robust, direct-from-investor allocation data and benchmarking capabilities. We are here to help you leverage comprehensive, connected and actionable private markets intelligence.
